summary: NASA's two fire satellite instruments do not count alike: VIIRS (since 2012) sees 1.4 to 3.3 times as much burning as MODIS (since 2000), so a fire record joined from both jumps in 2012 although nothing changed on the ground. FireLedger fixes that. It counts fire in a unit that is fair to both instruments (5 km² tiles with fire per day) and removes gas flares. It learns how MODIS counts translate into VIIRS counts in 2012–2019, when both flew. It proves the translation on 2020–2025, years the method never saw: a typical month was 7.5% off in Texas and Argentina, against 30% and 14% with one simple ratio. It then converts 2000–2011 with an uncertainty range. The result is one 25-year fire record for New York, California, Texas and Argentina. A web app puts it to work for fire services: where it burns, which months are unusual, how far fire stations are, where this week's fire weather is dangerous, and which stations to send.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

FireLedger is a web app built on one harmonized satellite fire record from November 2000 to December 2025, on the scale of VIIRS. It covers New York, California, Texas and Argentina. It opens on a 3D globe showing each region's 25 years of burning as red hexagons; a click flies in. Each region has pages named after the questions a fire chief or emergency planner asks:

1. Where does it burn? A map, the key numbers, every year, and a calendar of every month.

2. Is this unusual? Every month scored against the same month in the other years.

3. How far is help? The drive from the nearest of 8,788 fire stations to every place that burns.

4. Where should we be ready? The next seven days of fire weather per county (Meteomatics forecast, Fosberg Fire Weather Index), beside how much usually burns there and how far help is.

5. Who do we send? For one busy day, the stations to send to each fire so that the total drive time is smallest.

6. Can I trust it? How the two records became one, and the test that proves it.

7. Limits: what the numbers cannot tell you.

HOW THE HARMONIZATION WORKS

- Same cleaning for both NASA FIRMS archives: vegetation-fire detections only, confidence filters, and removal of industrial heat FIRMS does not flag (gas flares, refineries: spots seen night after night, year after year). In Texas this removed 38% of VIIRS detections; left in, they would have inflated the conversion.

- A unit fair to both instruments, the fire cell-day: a 5 km² hexagon counts once per day with any detection, so a fire that lights ten VIIRS pixels and one MODIS pixel counts the same.

- Days a satellite was switched off are found in the data and corrected for: "not seen" is not "no fire".

- Find the conversion (2012–2019, both satellites flying): a ratio for every area of about 12,000 km² and every month of the year, steadied where there is little fire, combined with a LightGBM model that places the fire inside each area.

- Test it (2020–2025, never shown to the method): estimates from MODIS alone against what VIIRS counted. A typical month was 7.5% off in Texas and Argentina (one simple ratio: 30% and 14%), 16% in California, and 41% in New York, which has little fire; there the app shows three-month periods instead of months.

- Convert 2000–2011, every map cell and month, each with an 80% uncertainty band. From February 2012 on, the record is what VIIRS observed.

WHY IT MATTERS

Fire services plan with history: where and when it burns, whether a season is unusual, where stations are too far away. A record that jumps in 2012 makes every trend across it wrong. FireLedger gives 25 comparable years and turns them into decisions: in Texas, 10.4% of the burning lies more than 30 minutes from a fire station, and on a busy day (27 February 2024, 3,323 detections) the optimized plan needs 3.6% less total drive time than sending each fire its nearest stations.

HOW IT WAS BUILT

Python: DuckDB and pandas for the data pipeline, Uber H3 hexagons, LightGBM and scikit-learn for the model, SciPy for routing (Dijkstra on US Census road data) and the dispatch plan (Hungarian algorithm), Plotly Dash for the web app, globe.gl for the 3D globe. Everything runs from public data on a laptop.

CREATIVITY AND FACTORS CONSIDERED

Instead of one multiplier, the conversion is learned by place and season and proven on unseen years, with an honest uncertainty range on every estimate. Pages are organized around responders' questions rather than datasets. We state the limits in the app: a detection is an observation, not a fire; a cloudy day is "not seen", not "no fire"; 2000–2011 cannot be checked directly because no VIIRS flew; drive times are estimates on main roads; the weather index says how a fire would spread, not that one will start.
